title: US Tells Allies to Expect Five-Year Arms Delays as BrahMos Exports Top $600M
subhead: The Iran war's drain on US munitions has turned into a global delivery crisis for allies, while India's BrahMos missile and South Korea's artillery exports keep filling the gap left by Western supply chains.

sections.heading: The munitions crunch goes global: allies warned of five-year delays
sections.body:
The US has formally warned allies to expect delays of as much as five years in deliveries of key weapons as it rebuilds its own depleted stocks, according to reporting by The Straits Times. Germany has asked Washington to accelerate delivery of Tomahawk cruise missiles and the ground-based Typhon launcher, but depleted US inventories mean manufacturer RTX's Raytheon is unlikely to fulfil the order within five years. Two officials said Eastern European nations reliant on US systems have also seen slippage since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran on February 28.

The scale of the drawdown is stark: the US is estimated to have used more than half of its most advanced Patriot variants, a third of its Tomahawks, and almost half of its precision strike missiles and THAAD interceptors. The Congressional Budget Office said the US has probably expended as much as two-thirds of its missile-defense interceptor inventory since June 2025. Reuters separately reported a September 15 CBO finding that the US will have a reduced interceptor inventory 'for several years.'

Ukraine's push for more Patriot interceptors ahead of winter is now caught in the same queue, and the issue is expected to dominate next week's UN meetings in New York.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the moment the Iran war's cost stops being an American accounting problem and becomes a NATO-wide readiness problem. Allies that built their air defense around US kit now face five-year waits — a structural opening for non-US suppliers.

sections.heading: India's BrahMos clears $600M in exports as Southeast Asia comes knocking
sections.body:
India's BrahMos supersonic cruise missile programme is set to cross $600 million in exports, with the Defence Ministry calling it a 'benchmark' for India's emerging arms export story. Rediff and other Indian outlets reported that New Delhi is now eyeing three Southeast Asian buyers, following the Philippines as the first confirmed customer and active interest from Indonesia, Vietnam, and Thailand.

The pitch is price: Indian reporting notes the missiles are offered at roughly one-fourth the price of global rivals. BrahMos is a Russo-Indian joint venture, giving it a supply line independent of Western producers now bottlenecked by the Iran war.

This builds on a year of steady Indian export momentum, with Indonesia's deal and a Vietnam agreement both reported earlier in 2026.
sections.whyItMatters: The BrahMos price point plus US backlog creates a rare opening for India in the mid-tier missile market. It signals the export map is splitting into two tiers — premium Western systems with long queues, and cheaper non-Western systems available now.

sections.heading: Pentagon locks in SM-6: $24.4B to Raytheon for five years of interceptors
sections.body:
The US Navy has awarded RTX's Raytheon a $24.4 billion contract for Standard Missile-6 (SM-6) interceptors, a five-year agreement with two additional option years. The Pentagon said the deal 'provides the defence industry with the long-term predictability needed to expand workforce capacity and secure critical supply chains.'

The SM-6 is a dual-role munition — capable of both anti-air and anti-surface strikes — built at Raytheon's Huntsville, Alabama facility. It follows a $20.7 billion provisional multiyear deal for AMRAAM missiles in late September and a $58.6 billion Patriot interceptor award to Lockheed Martin in July.

The awards trace directly to the Pentagon inspector general's finding that munitions expended in Operation Epic Fury (the Iran campaign) 'resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks.' The Wall Street Journal reported Trump has told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran by late November, which would mean further expenditure.
sections.whyItMatters: The Pentagon is trying to convert one-off wartime buys into multi-year industrial commitments. Predictability is the actual constraint on missile output — the money was never the bottleneck.

sections.heading: GM ships its first Patriot missile parts — automakers enter the defense supply chain
sections.body:
General Motors has delivered its first batch of Patriot interceptor components to Lockheed Martin, marking the automaker's formal entry into the missile supply chain, according to Anadolu Agency and Forbes. The company behind the Silverado is now producing parts for one of the US military's most in-demand interceptors.

The move echoes the 'Arsenal of Democracy' model of using civilian manufacturing capacity for wartime production, and comes as the Pentagon pushes contractors to expand output faster than their traditional suppliers can manage.
sections.whyItMatters: Bringing automakers into missile production is a bet that existing defense primes cannot scale fast enough alone. If it works, it rewires how the US industrial base responds to surge demand — and it is a template other sectors could follow.

sections.heading: Castelion's Blackbeard hypersonic flies on a Super Hornet for the first time
sections.body:
The US Navy released the first footage of Castelion's Blackbeard hypersonic strike missile carried by an F/A-18E/F Super Hornet during an actual flight test — the clearest public look yet at the weapon's integration with the carrier-based fighter. The footage, released by Naval Air Systems Command, shows two missiles mounted but does not show a launch.

Blackbeard is being developed by US startup Castelion, founded by former SpaceX employees, under the Navy's Multi-Mission Affordable Capacity Effector (MACE) programme. Exact speed and range are undisclosed, but the weapon is designed for hypersonic speeds (above Mach 5). The Navy is targeting early operational capability by 2027-2028 and plans to acquire thousands.

In September, the service announced a production deal worth up to $200 million for 444 missiles, following an order of 50 in June.
sections.whyItMatters: Blackbeard's defining feature is cost and mass production, not raw performance. The US is trying to field hypersonics as attritable, high-volume weapons rather than one-off exotics — a shift in what 'hypersonic' is for.

sections.heading: South Korea keeps winning Europe: Hanwha's Chunmoo lands in Croatia
sections.body:
South Korea's Hanwha Aerospace signed a deal to export 18 Chunmoo multiple launch rocket systems to Croatia in a contract worth around 640 billion won ($477 million / €410 million), per the Korea Times and Korea Herald. Croatia becomes the fourth European country to acquire the system, after Poland, Estonia, and Norway. It is the first major arms deal between Seoul and Zagreb, and the two defense ministries signed a broader memorandum on defense partnership.

The Chunmoo has an operational range up to 80 km and is designed to deliver both precision strikes and area cluster attacks. Korean defense exports have been one of the clearest beneficiaries of Europe's rearmament, with Poland alone ordering K2 tanks and K9 howitzers on a large scale.
sections.whyItMatters: Korea is consistently winning European artillery and armor contracts that Western primes cannot fill fast enough. Combined with the US delivery delays, it reinforces a market where speed of delivery now beats brand.

sections.heading: Ukraine's drone industry goes west: production moves into Belgium and Luxembourg
sections.body:
A Ukrainian drone manufacturer is moving to build inside Belgium and Luxembourg, responding to European demand for combat-proven drones rather than peacetime demonstrators, according to Euromaidan Press. The move is part of a wider pattern in which Ukraine's wartime drone expertise is being exported and industrialised abroad.

Ukraine has already signed drone or defense cooperation agreements with Denmark, Norway, and the Netherlands, plus a 10-year defense pact with Qatar and a declaration with Canada. CBS News reported Ukraine is ready to sign a drone defense agreement with the US that would expand testing and production of Ukrainian technology in America — though terms remain unannounced.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine is transitioning from a recipient of Western arms to an exporter of drone know-how. That is a genuine role reversal, and it positions Ukrainian firms inside European and US supply chains for the next decade.

bottomLine: The Iran war's munitions drain has now become a global arms-delivery crisis: the US has told allies to expect waits of up to five years on Patriot, Tomahawk, and Typhon systems, while it locks in multi-billion-dollar multi-year contracts ($24.4B for SM-6, $20.7B for AMRAAM) to rebuild. Into that gap step non-Western suppliers — India's BrahMos crossing $600 million in exports with three Southeast Asian buyers in view, and South Korea's Hanwha landing another European artillery sale in Croatia. The Pentagon is also experimenting with new industrial capacity, from GM building Patriot parts to the low-cost, mass-producible Blackbeard hypersonic. Going forward, expect the delivery queue and price, not platform prestige, to decide who wins the rearmament market.
sources: The Straits Times, Reuters, Congressional Budget Office (via reporting), TRT World, Defense News, Rediff, Latestly/Indian Defence Ministry, Anadolu Agency, Forbes, SOFX/The War Zone, NAVAIR, Korea Times, Korea Herald, Janes, Euromaidan Press, CBS News/Dronelife, Wall Street Journal (via TRT World), Pentagon Inspector General (via reporting)
